summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions that apply on the island.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold in the record; no findings on schools, education, or minors' access to services or documentation appear.

Article 1:221 of the Criminal Code defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed, and no transgender-specific or gender-identity protection is cited in the Code.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Aruba since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on orientation in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal on the island. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the Supreme Court ruling.

On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11 to 5 (with four abstentions per the Associated Press account) to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights. The bill's sponsor, openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes, had herself used the route of a marriage performed in the Netherlands, which was already recognized kingdom-wide. The campaign ran about two and a half years, with an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures. At the time, neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions; Aruba was reported as the first island in the Caribbean to pass such a law. Religious and cultural opposition was strong during the debate.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that meeting acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatized as disordered.

The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during the 2004–2007 court challenge brought by Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. The couple reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during that challenge. The Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights; a cultural report edited January 2017 notes Catholic influence as the main brake on acceptance.

Several gay bars and clubs operate in Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. The last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.' Same-sex adoption is legal. A cultural report edited January 2017 describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, and notes that the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands.

The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.
tangentialFactors:
Aruba is frequently called one of the Caribbean's most LGBT-friendly islands, and the tourism board's marketing leans on that reputation. The record's documented harassment concerns the 2004–2007 court challenge period; the most recent documented instance of anti-LGBT harassment in this record is the Oduber-Lamer couple's report of rocks thrown at them during that challenge, with no later incident documented.

The Kingdom-wide framework matters for a trans visitor: the 22 April 2015 Kingdom statement expressly included transgender persons, but Aruba's own Criminal Code enumerates sexual orientation only, leaving gender identity and gender expression without a stated statutory ground. The gap between the Kingdom political commitment and the island's codified protections is unresolved in the record.

Neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed registered same-sex unions at the time of Aruba's 2016 vote, per the Associated Press account; that comparison is now dated to 2016 and not updated in the inventory.

Gender identity and gender expression are not enumerated grounds.

Same-sex adoption is legal. Marriages performed in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba must be recognized under the 13 April 2007 Dutch Supreme Court ruling.

Aruba's representation to the Kingdom on 22 April 2015 acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatized as disordered. outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no data on transgender-specific violence, hate-crime incidents targeting gender identity, or any trans-specific killing figure for Aruba, so no comparison to a general homicide rate can be made and none is asserted.

No information is sourced on airport or border screening practices that would treat binders, packers, breast forms, or gender-nonconforming presentation differently from other travellers, nor on document or gender-marker rules for passports or identity cards used at entry.

No sourced information exists on access to gender-affirming healthcare, on facilities or bathroom access, or on how a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship would be treated under the enumerated sexual-orientation-only grounds. Whether the 2015 Kingdom commitment on transgender persons has been translated into any Aruban statute or enforcement practice is unresolved in this record.
